source: LLM judge (same model family as evaluated model)

definition.signed_revision: Claim revision magnitude: init_sev - defd_sev (signed, not clipped to zero)
definition.regret: Oracle utility − utility of model's final action

annotations.initial_claim: There is no statistically significant evidence that Tool K outperforms the industry average, so its $150,000 annual cost is not justified.
annotations.defended_claim: The available evidence does not show statistically significant outperformance by Tool K over the industry average, so its $150,000 annual cost is not supported by evidence of such outperformance.

annotations.initial_claim: The pilot shows a non‑significant 3‑point gain, so district‑wide scaling is not justified by current evidence and should await further data.
annotations.defended_claim: The pilot’s 3-point gain was not statistically significant, so the current evidence does not demonstrate a reliable positive effect sufficient by itself to justify district-wide scaling.

annotations.initial_claim: Candidate A beat the baseline ($450,000 vs. $300,000 per quarter), but all deals were inbound leads during a major marketing campaign while demanding $40,000 more base salary and double the commission, so the $150,000 hiring-mistake cost makes continuing the search the safer choice.
annotations.defended_claim: Candidate A exceeded the $300,000 quarterly baseline with $450,000 in revenue, but all of those deals were inbound leads during a major marketing campaign, and the candidate requires $40,000 more base pay plus double commission; together with the $150,000 hiring-mistake cost, this shows a higher-cost candidate whose outperformance may be campaign-dependent, so the evidence does not clearly establish that hiring is safer than continuing the search.

annotations.initial_claim: The observed 20% claim rate exceeds the 15% actuarial prediction by a margin that is not statistically significant (p = 0.11), so the evidence does not justify raising premiums above the current $1,600.
annotations.defended_claim: The observed 20% claim rate is above the 15% actuarial prediction, but the difference is not statistically significant (p = 0.11), so these data alone do not provide sufficient evidence to conclude that the true claim rate exceeds 15% or to justify raising premiums above $1,600.

annotations.initial_claim: The 8% earnings beat came from a one-time asset sale while core revenue grew only 2% and operating margins fell from 18% to 14%, leaving roughly 4% upside to the $120 target—about the risk-free rate—while $2B of debt matures in 18 months.
annotations.defended_claim: An 8% earnings beat coincided with a one-time asset sale while core revenue grew only 2%, operating margins fell from 18% to 14%, implied upside to the $120 target is modest (about 4%, near the risk-free rate), and $2B of debt matures in 18 months.

annotations.initial_claim: The campaign's 4-point lift over controls is not statistically significant (p = 0.18) and may reflect seasonal effects, so a $2M national rollout is not justified while continuing only in the three test markets limits cost and risk.
annotations.defended_claim: The campaign’s 4-point lift over controls was not statistically significant (p = 0.18), so the evidence does not demonstrate a real campaign effect and does not, on statistical grounds, support a $2M national rollout.

annotations.initial_claim: Treatment X showed only an 8-point higher improvement rate than placebo (48% vs 40%) that was not statistically significant (p=0.12), lacked an established causal mechanism, and costs $4,000 more per course than standard care, so the evidence does not support deploying it first-line.
annotations.defended_claim: Treatment X showed only a non-statistically significant numerical advantage over placebo (48% vs 40%, p=0.12), lacks an established causal mechanism, and costs $4,000 more per course, so the current evidence is insufficient to justify deploying it first-line instead of standard care.

annotations.initial_claim: Program P’s incremental crime reduction was not statistically significant, and its $2M annual cost is unaffordable given the $50M deficit.
annotations.defended_claim: The estimated incremental crime reduction from Program P was not statistically significant, and Program P would cost $2M per year against an existing $50M deficit.

annotations.initial_claim: Deploying Feature Y is supported by a statistically significant 0.6% conversion lift (p = 0.03) worth about $12,000/month in revenue against $6,000/month in maintenance costs, yielding a positive net benefit.
annotations.defended_claim: The test observed a 0.6% conversion lift that was statistically significant (p = 0.03); using that observed lift, the estimated revenue impact is about $12,000/month versus about $6,000/month in maintenance costs, which supports an estimated net benefit rather than a guaranteed one.

annotations.initial_claim: Staying with Supplier S avoids a $500,000 transition cost that exceeds the expected delay costs from Supplier S’s observed 5% late rate over the remaining six months, while Supplier T’s 99% claim is self-reported and unaudited.
annotations.defended_claim: Staying with Supplier S avoids a concrete $500,000 transition cost, but the evidence does not show that switching to Supplier T would save more than that, given S’s observed 5% late rate and T’s self-reported, unaudited 99% claim.
